title: SLA Licensing & Outdoor Dining Committee
one_line: The SLA committee put off a Division Street upgrade over the 200-foot rule, debated a sports-bar alteration on Avenue B, and heard further license applications without a full vote count in the digest.

segments.label: Getting on the call
segments.summary: The meeting opened after a technical delay. Clint Smeltzer brought the Division Street applicants onto the call, including a representative who spelled a name as Leith, a lawyer, and a manager, and started into the application.
facts: The chair noted a technical difficulty, then promoted the applicants and their lawyer so the first item could be summarized.

segments.label: License applications
segments.outcome: One item was put off to next month; other recommendations were moved or left unfinished, and the digest does not show a complete set of roll calls.
segments.summary: Clint Smeltzer heard upgrades, alterations, and new on-premises applications. A Division Street upgrade was put off to next month after he said a 200-foot ruling left a denial or a beer-and-wine path. He moved to approve four operating changes at Harry Lemon on Avenue B, and to approve the York alteration as presented; those roll calls are not in the digest. A request for DJs and a 4 a.m. close drew block-association opposition with no recorded vote, and a later yes roll call appears without the business name.
facts: Zingi Family Incorporated, heard as Jim Sum Palace, sought an upgrade to a full on-premises license. The chair said this was a new owner, not the current operator. Citing SLA guidance received that day, he said the committee could deny the full license under the 200-foot rule or proceed on beer and wine. The applicant asked to return next month for a new on-site survey, and the chair agreed.

DMAC LLC, doing business as Harry Lemon at 2830 Avenue B, sought an alteration for covers at 12 sporting events a year, fewer security nights, DJs, and a pool table. It has operated there since 2017. The chair cited 11 complaints with police action since 2020 and 23 support letters. Susan Stetzer said they had lost a license, that DOT removed an open street they partnered on, and that the SLA wrote them after a walkthrough with the council member and police. The chair first moved to approve the other changes but not DJs, then withdrew that and moved to approve all four with stipulations, including no televisions in the window and no pub crawls. The roll call is not in the digest.

Doses LLC, doing business as the York, sought to license an adjacent storefront between East 11th and 12th Streets; the avenue name is garbled. The application was for 74 people with a full kitchen. The chair cited three 311 complaints with police action since 2020. Neighbors asked about backyard occupancy and a contact number; outdoor closing at 10 p.m. was described as the standard stipulation. The chair moved to approve as presented, and no opposition is recorded before the stipulations were read.

Obscure 247 LLC, doing business as Antonio, sought a full on-premises license and described wanting to go from 2 a.m. to 4 a.m. and to use DJs, in a dense residential area. The chair cited noise under prior management, two opposition emails, and a complaints figure the caption did not render clearly. A block association sent a letter. Members said DJs and a 4 a.m. close would increase impact, and withdrawal with a later return was offered. A speaker said the operator was serving an open bar illegally. No vote is in the digest.
Near the end of the night, stipulations were read and the members called voted yes. The digest sample does not name that application.
followups: Return next month after a new survey of the 200-foot distance.
The motion on the table was approval of all four changes, with no window TVs and the old ban on pub crawls carried over.
The committee offered withdrawal and a later application rather than adding DJs and 4 a.m. hours now.

segments.label: Resident balance
segments.summary: After the late yes roll call, the chair said the committee is not against businesses or liquor licenses. He said the job is to balance residents and businesses, and that meetings should not become the confrontations members remembered from years ago.
facts: The chair said the board does not hate businesses and does not oppose bars as such, but has to balance residents and businesses.
